targetQuery: unit testing fundamentals c# xunit arrange act assert
comparedAgainst: https://xunit.net/docs/getting-started/v3/getting-started (xUnit.net, fetched and read in full) — the article's own primary source for [Fact]/[Theory]. It defines the two attributes procedurally ('always true'/'invariant condition' vs 'only true for a particular set of data') and states 'each theory with its data set is a separate test', but never discusses what a passing test does and does not prove, never shows a brittle test, and never runs a worked example end to end with real output.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/testing/unit-testing-best-practices (Microsoft Learn, fetched and read in full) — the article's own primary source for AAA and naming. It covers the same naming convention (method/scenario/expected-behavior) and the same AAA discipline ('reduce the opportunity for assertions to intermix with code in the Act task'), but its worked example throughout is Roy Osherove's StringCalculator kata. This article deliberately does not reuse that running example (per the editorial brief's 'do not reuse a source's running example' rule) and instead builds an original GradeCalculator/LetterGrade scenario with its own boundary-testing exercises, none of which appear on the MS page.

General familiarity with the genre of beginner C#/xUnit unit-testing walkthroughs (typical Calculator.Add()-style tutorials that stop at 'here is how you write a [Fact]'): none of that class of tutorial addresses what a green test does and doesn't demonstrate, or shows a real behavior-preserving refactor breaking a test asserted on an incidental detail. Disclosure: this session's WebSearch quota was exhausted partway through the review (200/200 used across the conversation before a planned third live search for a specific competing blog post), so this third comparison rests on general domain knowledge of the genre rather than a freshly fetched, named URL — flagged here rather than fabricating a specific source I did not actually re-verify live.
justification: This is a strong, original entry point for the pillar. The opening paragraph and 'What a unit test proves — and what it doesn't' section do real intellectual work that the two official sources it cites do not attempt: it lists exactly three things a passing test demonstrates, states plainly what it does not (correctness on untried inputs, the rest of the program, future edits), and grounds the claim in xUnit's own procedural language ('invariant condition') and Microsoft's own reasoning ('protection against regression') rather than a generic 'testing is good' platitude — this is honest, not inflated, and it does not overclaim what a green suite proves. Both fetched primary sources (xUnit's Getting Started page, MS Learn's Best practices page) were spot-checked quote-by-quote against the article's citations and every one matches: the Fact/Theory definitions, the naming-convention's three parts, the AAA guidance, and Bill Wake's 2001 authorship of the name (confirmed on xp123.com) are all accurately represented. The File-based apps citation and the EqualityAsserts.cs claim (that the precision overload rounds both sides before comparing) were independently verified against the live pages and match exactly. The GradeCalculator/LetterGrade/ReportCard example is not a reskin of the classic 'add two numbers' or StringCalculator examples every xUnit tutorial (including its own MS Learn source) uses — it is original, and the brittle-test narrative (a ToString format change from F2 to F1 breaking a string-equality assertion that pins the display format instead of the average and grade) is a genuine, non-contrived lesson about testing behavior vs. incidental implementation detail, with a real fixed test shown passing against the same F1-formatted code that broke the naive one. `node tools/run-code.mjs` confirms PASS, blocks=16, executed=7, matching the writer's claim, and the toolchain sentence ('.NET 10 SDK (10.0.401) on Windows 11, x64') was independently checked against this machine's `dotnet --version`/`dotnet --info` and is accurate; it sits beside the first real code block, not the opening paragraph. Structure is not templated against the pillar's only sibling, test-doubles.md: this article opens with a concrete run-and-observe moment rather than a two-sentence direct definition, uses eight H2s with no H3 subdivision (test-doubles nests five H3s under one H2), and its three exercises ('Find the bug', 'Predict, don't run', 'Prove it') are different forms from and are interleaved through the body rather than clustered, matching the brief's variety rule without repeating the sibling's heading shapes or its 'Name the double'/'A mock test that cannot fail'/'Loosen the strict test'/'Write the contract' exercise set. All three named exercise types (find-the-bug, predict-the-output, prove-it) are genuinely different in mechanics, and none leaks its answer outside the collapsed solution: the find-the-bug exercise shows the buggy program and its failure output as the puzzle's own given data (the point is to diagnose from the failure, not to be told the diagnosis), the predict-the-output exercise shows no output panel before its solution, and the prove-it exercise states no answer before its solution. As the pillar's order-1, prerequisites-[] entry point, it does not assume prior testing knowledge: it defines a unit test's guarantees from first principles, links '[unit tests](/glossary/#unit-test)' at first use, explains the `#:package` file-based-app directive it depends on, and explicitly defers test doubles to test-doubles.md rather than assuming or half-explaining them. No filler, no keyword stuffing, no ad or consent/analytics code. Held to 9.0 rather than higher for two minor sourcing nits below, and reserved from a full 10 because a review that finds literally nothing is not the bar the role expects.

issues.location: "Arrange, Act, Assert" section, the clause '...recommending that each stay visually separate so "assertions [don't] intermix with code in the Act task"'
issues.problem: The bracketed insertion reverses the source's grammar rather than just supplying a missing word: Microsoft Learn's actual sentence is 'The pattern also helps to reduce the opportunity for assertions to intermix with code in the Act task' (a description of what AAA achieves), not a recommendation phrased with 'don't'. Presenting it as a direct quote with an inserted negation risks reading as changed source text rather than a legitimate ellipsis/bracket edit.
issues.fixLooksLike: Paraphrase instead of quoting the fragment: e.g. recommending that each stay visually separate, which Microsoft's own guidance frames as reducing 'the opportunity for assertions to intermix with code in the Act task' (drop the inserted "don't" and quote the source's actual wording, or summarize without quotation marks).

issues.location: "Naming a test so the failure explains itself" section: 'The exact word order is not sacred — some teams write BDD-flavored names such as `Should_ReturnMean_When_GivenThreeScores` instead.'
issues.problem: This is a claim about what other teams commonly do, stated without a source — the same shape of claim the editorial brief's pilot-round lessons flag ('No "what most people think" claims unless sourced'). It is plausible (Given-When-Then/BDD-style naming is a real, documented convention) but nothing in the sources list supports it.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either cite a source for BDD-style test naming (e.g. a well-known BDD/SpecFlow reference) or rephrase as the article's own observation rather than a claim about other teams' practice: 'The exact word order is not sacred; a BDD-flavored name such as `Should_ReturnMean_When_GivenThreeScores` would carry the same three parts.'
